title: How xomtra keeps your home safe
desc: xomtra only reads Home Assistant, lets in only the people and devices you allow and keeps the history on your machine. How the code does it.
lead: Home Assistant history shows when people are at home and how they live. xomtra treats it that way: it only reads, it gives each person exactly the access you choose, and it keeps the data on your own machine. Everything below is open source, so you do not have to take our word for it.

b: xomtra reads states, history and statistics from Home Assistant and never calls its services. Your AI assistant talks only to xomtra and gets read only tools over xomtra's own copy of the data. There is no tool that switches, opens or sets anything.

Home Assistant has no read only tokens: every token can do what its user can. The guarantee is xomtra's code, which you can read. With Docker, connect xomtra as a separate Home Assistant user without admin rights; automated tests check that such a user cannot change anything.
Entities you do not want stored or analysed get a label in Home Assistant.

Home Assistant, or Microsoft Entra ID if you choose it, only confirms who is signing in. The role comes from xomtra and is kept in its own database: Home Assistant administrators always have xomtra.Admin, a new account has no role, and anyone else gets in only after an administrator gives them one on the admin page Access. xomtra knows people by the fixed ID of their account, never by a name or an e-mail address, which can change.

In your network, each device gets a personal token from the admin page MCP tokens. It is shown once; xomtra keeps only its fingerprint, not the token itself. Like a long-lived token in Home Assistant, a token belongs to the person who issued it and has their role; an administrator can limit it to xomtra.Reader. When the role changes or the person loses access, their tokens follow within 30 seconds. Everyone can revoke their own tokens, and an administrator any token.

From the internet, Claude connects through your Home Assistant account, by default only with two-factor authentication. Before the sign-in xomtra always shows a consent page that names the client, so a link sent by someone else cannot connect their Claude to your home.

Right after sign-in xomtra revokes the Home Assistant token it received and keeps its own session, 180 days by default. Claude gets access tokens valid for at most 60 minutes; xomtra checks every renewal against that session and the person's role, never through Home Assistant. On the page Access, Disconnect ends a sign-in within a minute and Disconnect everywhere ends every session of a person, the admin page included.

If xomtra reads Home Assistant with an administrator token, it loads Home Assistant's list of users every 5 minutes: a removed or deactivated user loses access within minutes. With a token without admin rights, as the Docker guide recommends, xomtra cannot see that list. So when you remove someone in Home Assistant, also click Disconnect everywhere for them in xomtra and take their role away.

Roles decide what the AI may see. By default a reader does not see people, locations, cameras, locks, alarms or the free text of attributes; these are filtered out in the database, before any answer is put together. An administrator adjusts this list on the page Hidden from Reader, and xomtra records who changed it and why.

The MCP server, the part the AI talks to, holds no Home Assistant token and no key to the stored one, so even someone who took it over could not control your home. Only the data import and the admin page talk to Home Assistant, and only to read. The exception is the add-on, where everything shares one container and the Supervisor's token; that is why its MCP port is meant only for your own network.

When the AI asks in SQL, three layers check the query: only one read query over the views its role allows, a database opened read only without access to files or the network, and views that already leave out what the role must not see.
Every call is recorded: who asked, what, and whether it was allowed. If the record cannot be stored, the AI gets an error instead of the data.

You sign in to the admin page with your Home Assistant account, or with Microsoft Entra ID; in the add-on straight from Home Assistant. After sign-in xomtra revokes the Home Assistant token it received, so it keeps no Home Assistant token of the person who signed in. The session is kept in xomtra's database: signing out ends it, and a changed role applies from the next click.

Every page states which roles may open it, and the server checks that on every request. A reader sees only their own MCP tokens and how to connect clients; anything else is refused and written to the audit log.
A new installation is opened with a setup link that works only once and for at most 24 hours. Only someone who may run a command on the server can create one.
By default the admin page answers only from your local network, and in the add-on only through Home Assistant. It loads nothing from other sites and protects every form against forged requests.

sections.h: In your network, or carefully on the internet

ul: Home Assistant add-on: the MCP port is for clients in your local network (Claude Desktop, Claude Code and others). It is plain HTTP, so use it only in a network you trust; it is not meant to be opened to the internet.
Docker: HTTPS in your network with xomtra's own local certificate authority.

Access from the internet (for Claude.ai): xomtra sits behind Caddy with a Let's Encrypt certificate. Anyone can reach only the sign-in pages; the data endpoints answer only to Claude's published addresses. You sign in with a Home Assistant account, or with Microsoft Entra ID if you choose it.

b: Release images are built only by GitHub Actions from the public code, scanned for known vulnerabilities and signed with cosign, so you can check that an image comes from the xomtra repository. A release ships the very images that passed the tests. Commits and release tags are signed.
Keys and passwords are generated on your machine at install; the code has no default secrets. Services run without root rights, with a read only file system.

The history stays on the machine where xomtra runs, and xomtra itself sends it nowhere. What your AI client fetches to answer you goes to its provider under your own account and its terms. Roles and labels decide what it can fetch.

xomtra binds its data to one Home Assistant instance. If a connection leads to another one, for example after you reinstall Home Assistant, xomtra writes nothing from it until an administrator decides on the page HA instance: keep the data and fix the connection, or delete them and start over with the new instance.

xomtra also gives the AI guardrails for its answers. The fixed core always applies: only values fetched from xomtra, no conclusions about a person's presence, sleep or health unless you ask, no jokes about accidents or threats to life and health, and nothing discriminatory, political or religious. On top of it comes the set of answer guidelines you choose on the admin page MCP setup. The sets are stored on your machine, only administrators can change them, and no text for the model comes from xomtra.com. The guardrails guide the model; they are not a security boundary.
